abstract: Alex Tabarrok reads the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey AI supplement as direct firm-side evidence that AI has not yet moved aggregate employment. The contribution is not new data — the figures are Census published tables — but the two-wave comparison. Census has asked firms twice whether AI use changed their total employment over the preceding six months. In the December 2023 to February 2024 wave, when roughly 5% of firms used AI, 2.8% reported increases, 2.6% reported decreases, and 94.6% reported no change. In the November 2025 to February 2026 wave, with adoption roughly tripled, 2.3% reported increases, 2.0% reported decreases, and 95.7% reported no change. Adoption rose sharply while the share of firms reporting any AI-attributed employment effect fell slightly, and the firms reporting an effect remain roughly evenly split between hiring more and hiring fewer. Tabarrok notes results are similar across firm sizes and that employment-weighting gives essentially the same answer as firm-weighting. He also reports the one countervailing trend: among the minority of adopters where AI has displaced some employee tasks, the intensity of that substitution is rising. Written for a general audience on Marginal Revolution; the author discloses using AI tools to produce the post.
keyFindings: Census asked firms twice how AI use affected total employment over the prior six months. Dec 2023-Feb 2024: 2.8% increased, 2.6% decreased, 94.6% no change. Nov 2025-Feb 2026: 2.3% increased, 2.0% decreased, 95.7% no change.
Adoption roughly tripled between the two waves (about 5% of firms using AI in the first, about 18% in the second) while the share reporting no employment change rose from 94.6% to 95.7%.
Firms reporting an employment effect are split roughly evenly between increases and decreases in both waves — the net effect is positive but within rounding of zero.
Results are similar across firm sizes, and employment-weighted estimates give essentially the same result as the firm-weighted estimates reported.
Information is the only sector where fewer than 92% of firms report no change.
Among AI-using firms, 44% say AI supplemented or enhanced work an employee already does, 10% say it performed a task an employee used to do, and 11% say it introduced a task no one had been doing.
Among generative AI users: 85% cite writing or editing documents and email, about 50% searching for information, 45% summarizing documents, and 13% coding.
64% of adopters changed nothing about the business in order to use AI; 15% trained existing staff, 15% built new workflows, and just over 1% hired anyone with AI skills.

Countervailing trend: among firms where AI has taken over employee tasks, the share reporting it took over 'a large number' of tasks rose from 2.4% to 7.1% and 'a moderate number' from 13% to 22% — but this group is about a tenth of adopters, who are about a fifth of firms.

Census BTOS AI use rose from 3.7% (September 2023) to about 10% (late 2025) on the original two-week production question; the November 2025 rewording to any business function lifted measured adoption to about 18%.
methodology: Secondary analysis of published Census Bureau Business Trends and Outlook Survey tables, including the biweekly AI question introduced September 2023 and the two AI supplements that carry the six-month employment-effect module (reference periods December 2023 to February 2024 and November 2025 to February 2026). BTOS surveys hundreds of thousands of businesses; the 2026 supplement drew roughly 117,000 responses weighted to represent about 1.2 million sampled US businesses. Tabarrok reports firm-weighted estimates and states that employment-weighting produces essentially the same result. No regression, no counterfactual, no causal identification — the argument rests on the direct survey question asking firms to attribute employment change to AI. Author discloses using Fable and ChatGPT Sol in producing the post.
qualifiers: This is blog commentary by a professional economist, not peer-reviewed work, and every number traces to Census published tables already available directly. The two waves are not a clean panel: the adoption question was reworded in November 2025 from AI used to produce goods and services in the past two weeks to AI used in any business function, so the population of 'AI users' being compared across waves is not identical and skews toward lighter, more peripheral use in the later wave. The employment-effect estimate is firm self-attribution — a firm that slowed hiring for several reasons at once need not name AI as one of them, and BTOS has no mechanism to check the attribution against payroll. Because it counts firms rather than jobs, the 2.0% cannot be read as a share of employment lost. The Information-sector figure is stated as a bound (fewer than 92% report no change), not a point estimate. Tabarrok's own reported substitution-intensity trend cuts against his headline and he flags the small base it sits on. The finding is also consistent with a null that is simply early: BTOS captures the six months to February 2026, and adoption at about a fifth of firms leaves most of the economy untreated.
